questions.question:
Let $R$ be the region in the complex plane defined by $1 \le \text{Im}(z) \le 3$ and $|z| < 4$.

Which diagram best represents the region $R$? (Dashed lines/curves are excluded boundaries; solid lines are included.)
questions.answer: $\text{Im}(z)=1$ and $\text{Im}(z)=3$ are included (solid horizontal lines), while $|z|=4$ is excluded (dashed arc). The region is the horizontal strip between $y=1$ and $y=3$ inside the circle of radius 4. Only (B) has both lines solid and the arc dashed.

questions.question:
A driving manual contains the following statement:

'If someone is bad at driving, then they will never miss an exit.'

Which of the following is logically equivalent to this statement?
questions.answer: A statement is equivalent to its contrapositive. 'If $P$ then $Q$' has contrapositive 'if not $Q$ then not $P$', with $P$ = 'bad at driving', $Q$ = 'never misses an exit'. Not $Q$ = 'misses an exit', so the contrapositive is 'If someone misses an exit, then they are not bad at driving' (D).
options: If someone is good at driving, then they will never miss an exit.
If someone is not bad at driving, then they will miss an exit.
If someone misses an exit, then they are bad at driving.
If someone misses an exit, then they are not bad at driving.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct expression for $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{5-4x-x^2}}$?
questions.answer: Complete the square: $5-4x-x^2 = 9-(x+2)^2$, so $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{3^2-(x+2)^2}} = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)+c$ (B).

questions.question:
A complex number $z = x+iy$ is defined such that $\text{Re}\left(\dfrac{1}{z}\right)=\dfrac12$.

Which of the following circles in the complex plane must $z$ always lie on?
questions.answer: $\dfrac1z=\dfrac{x-iy}{x^2+y^2}$, so $\text{Re}\left(\dfrac1z\right)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}=\dfrac12$. Then $x^2-2x+y^2=0$, i.e. $(x-1)^2+y^2=1$ (A).

questions.question:
The vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are given by $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix}\sin\theta\\ \cos\theta\\ \tan\theta\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix}\text{cosec}\,\theta\\ \sec\theta\\ \cot\theta\end{pmatrix}$, where $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

For how many values of $\theta$ is $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{p}}\,\mathbf{q}$ a unit vector?
questions.answer:
$\text{proj}_{\mathbf p}\mathbf q=\dfrac{\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q}{|\mathbf p|^2}\mathbf p$, with magnitude $\dfrac{|\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q|}{|\mathbf p|}$.

$\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q = 1+1+1=3$ and $|\mathbf p|^2=\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$, so $|\mathbf p|=|\sec\theta|$.

The magnitude is $3|\cos\theta|=1$, so $\cos\theta=\pm\frac13$. On $[0,2\pi]$ this gives 4 values of $\theta$ (none make $\sin\theta$ or $\cos\theta$ zero), so (D).

questions.question:
The diagram below shows the complex number $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ on the Argand diagram.

Which of the following diagrams best shows the position of $\dfrac{ir^2}{z}$?
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{ir^2}{z}=\dfrac{ir^2}{r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)}=ir(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)=i\bar z$, since $\bar z=r(\cos\theta-i\sin\theta)$.

So take the conjugate of $z$ (reflect in the real axis, same modulus $r>1$), then multiply by $i$ (rotate $90^\circ$ anticlockwise). $z$ is in the second quadrant, $\bar z$ in the third, and rotating by $90^\circ$ puts the point in the fourth quadrant at distance $r>1$ from the origin: (A).

questions.question:
Consider the statement:

$\forall\, p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^+,\ \exists\, m,n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $\sqrt{p+q}=\sqrt m+\sqrt n$.

Which of the following could be used as a counterexample to disprove this statement?
questions.answer:
A counterexample needs $p,q\in\mathbb Z^+$ for which no positive integers $m,n$ work. (A) is not allowed ($-2\notin\mathbb Z^+$). For (B), $\sqrt9=3=\sqrt4+\sqrt1$; for (C), $\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2=\sqrt2+\sqrt8$.

For (D): suppose $\sqrt6=\sqrt m+\sqrt n$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z^+$. Each of $\sqrt m,\sqrt n$ is at least $1$, so each is at most $\sqrt6-1\approx1.45$, giving $m,n\in\{1,2\}$. The possible sums are $\sqrt1+\sqrt1=2$, $1+\sqrt2\approx2.414$ and $2\sqrt2\approx2.83$, none equal to $\sqrt6\approx2.449$. So no such $m,n$ exist, and $p=2,\ q=4$ is a counterexample: (D).

questions.question:
It is known that the vector $\mathbf r=\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to $a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k$, where $a,b,c\ne0$.

Which of the following vectors is NOT perpendicular to $\mathbf r$?
questions.answer:
Perpendicular to $\mathbf r$ means dot product with $\mathbf r$ is $0$. Given $a-b+2c=0$.

(A) $(a+c)-(b+c)+2c=a-b+2c=0$.

(B) $b-a-2c=-(a-b+2c)=0$.

(C) $b-a+2(a-b+c)=a-b+2c=0$.

(D) $(2c-a)-(b-2c)+2(a+b-c)=a+b+2c=(a-b+2c)+2b=2b\neq0$.

So (D) is not perpendicular.

questions.question:
The complex number $z$ is defined such that $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le\text{Arg}(z-i)\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Which of the following describes the set of values that $\text{Arg}(z^2+1)$ can take?
questions.answer:
$z^2+1=(z+i)(z-i)$, so $\arg(z^2+1)=\arg(z+i)+\arg(z-i)$. Here $z$ lies in the wedge with vertex $i$ bounded by the rays at $\pm\frac\pi4$ to the horizontal ($z\ne i$, since $z^2+1\ne0$).

Upper ray ($\arg(z-i)=\frac\pi4$): $\arg(z+i)$ runs from just under $\frac\pi2$ (near $z=i$) down towards $\frac\pi4$ as $|z|\to\infty$, so the sum is less than $\frac{3\pi}4$ and approaches $\frac\pi2$.

Lower ray ($\arg(z-i)=-\frac\pi4$): $\arg(z+i)$ falls from just under $\frac\pi2$ towards $-\frac\pi4$, so the sum is greater than $-\frac\pi2$ and starts near $\frac\pi4$.

The sum takes every value in between, so $-\frac\pi2<\text{Arg}(z^2+1)<\frac{3\pi}4$ (B).

questions.question:
The graph below shows the derivative of the velocity $v$ of a particle as a function of its displacement $x$, where $x\ge0$.

It is known that if the particle is at $x=0$, it will be stationary and will not move.

Which of the following graphs best shows the acceleration of the particle as a function of its displacement?
questions.answer:
Acceleration is $a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$. Integrating $\frac{dv}{dx}$ with $v=0$ at $x=0$: $v$ rises from $0$ to a maximum at $x=2$, then falls back to $0$ at $x=4$ (flat there since $\frac{dv}{dx}=0$) and then rises again, with $v\ge0$ throughout.

So $a=v\frac{dv}{dx}$ has the sign of $\frac{dv}{dx}$: positive for $0<x<2$, zero at $x=2$, negative for $2<x<4$, and it is zero at $x=0$ and $x=4$ (where $v=0$ and $\frac{dv}{dx}=0$) before turning positive again. This matches (A).

questions.question:
The complex numbers $w$ and $z$ are given in polar form by $w=8\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}+i\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)$ and $z=2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

Find the modulus and principal argument of $\dfrac wz$.
questions.answer:
Dividing in polar form, moduli divide and arguments subtract:

$\left|\frac wz\right|=\frac82=4$ and $\arg\frac wz=\frac{3\pi}4-\frac\pi6=\frac{9\pi-2\pi}{12}=\frac{7\pi}{12}$, which lies in $(-\pi,\pi]$, so $\text{Arg}\frac wz=\frac{7\pi}{12}$.

(The original paper wrote $w=8e^{3i\pi/4}$ and $z=2e^{i\pi/6}$; here it is restated in polar form.)

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int(\tan^2x+1)\sec^2x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $u=\tan x$, $du=\sec^2x\,dx$:

$\int(u^2+1)\,du=\frac13u^3+u+c=\frac13\tan^3x+\tan x+c$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2}{4+x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{x^2}{4+x^2}=\dfrac{(x^2+4)-4}{4+x^2}=1-\dfrac{4}{4+x^2}$, so

$\int\frac{x^2}{4+x^2}dx=x-4\cdot\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2+c=x-2\tan^{-1}\frac x2+c$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int x\cos x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
By parts with $u=x$, $v'=\cos x$ ($u'=1$, $v=\sin x$):

$\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x-\int\sin x\,dx=x\sin x+\cos x+c$.

questions.question:
Two lines are given by
$\mathbf r_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\14\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf r_2=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$, where $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$.

Show that the lines intersect, and find their point of intersection.
questions.answer:
Equate components:

$i$: $1+\lambda=-6+2\mu\Rightarrow\lambda-2\mu=-7$ (1)

$j$: $-2-\lambda=3-\mu\Rightarrow\mu-\lambda=5$ (2)

(1)+(2): $-\mu=-2$, so $\mu=2$ and $\lambda=-3$.

Check $k$: LHS $=14+3(-3)=5$; RHS $=-1+3(2)=5$. The $k$-components agree, so the lines intersect.

Point: $\mathbf r_2$ at $\mu=2$ is $(-6+4,\ 3-2,\ -1+6)=(-2,1,5)$.

questions.question:
Two lines have direction vectors $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

Determine the acute angle between the lines, giving your answer correct to the nearest degree.
questions.answer:
$\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2=2+1+9=12$, $|\mathbf d_1|=\sqrt{11}$, $|\mathbf d_2|=\sqrt{14}$.

$\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{11}\sqrt{14}}\approx0.967$, so $\theta\approx15^\circ$ (to the nearest degree).

questions.question: Show that if $n$ is an integer, then $n^2+7n+6$ is even.
questions.answer:
$n^2+7n+6=(n+6)(n+1)$.

If $n$ is even, $n+6$ is even, so the product is even. If $n$ is odd, $n+1$ is even, so the product is even. In either case $n^2+7n+6$ is even.

questions.question: Given that $n^2+7n+6$ is even for every integer $n$, determine, with justification, the number of integer solutions to the equation $(n^2+7n+6)^7-16n^5=3$.
questions.answer: Since $n^2+7n+6$ is even, $(n^2+7n+6)^7$ is even. Also $16n^5$ is even. So the left side is even, but $3$ is odd. Hence there are $0$ integer solutions.

questions.question:
Find the values of $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that
$$\frac{3x^2-6x+13}{(x-5)(x^2+4)}=\frac{A}{x-5}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}.$$
questions.answer:
$3x^2-6x+13=A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)(x-5)$.

$x=5$: $58=29A\Rightarrow A=2$.

$x=0$: $13=4A-5C=8-5C\Rightarrow C=-1$.

Coefficient of $x^2$: $A+B=3\Rightarrow B=1$.

So $A=2,\ B=1,\ C=-1$.

questions.question: Given that $\dfrac{3x^2-6x+13}{(x-5)(x^2+4)}=\dfrac{2}{x-5}+\dfrac{x-1}{x^2+4}$, find $\displaystyle\int\frac{3x^2-6x+13}{(x-5)(x^2+4)}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $\int\left(\frac2{x-5}+\frac{x}{x^2+4}-\frac1{x^2+4}\right)dx=2\ln|x-5|+\frac12\ln(x^2+4)-\frac12\tan^{-1}\frac x2+c$.

questions.question:
An object moving in simple harmonic motion has displacement $x$ m and velocity $v$ m s$^{-1}$, and its motion satisfies $v^2=27-18x-9x^2$.

Find the centre of motion and the amplitude.
questions.answer:
The speed is zero at the extremes: $27-18x-9x^2=0\Rightarrow x^2+2x-3=0\Rightarrow(x+3)(x-1)=0$, so $x=-3$ or $x=1$.

Centre of motion: $x=\frac{-3+1}2=-1$. Amplitude: $\frac{1-(-3)}2=2$ m.

questions.question:
An object moves in simple harmonic motion with $v^2=27-18x-9x^2$ (centre $x=-1$, amplitude $2$ m).

Determine the period and hence find the distance that the particle will travel in $30\pi$ seconds.
questions.answer:
$v^2=-9(x^2+2x-3)=9\left(4-(x+1)^2\right)=n^2\left(A^2-(x-c)^2\right)$, so $n=3$ and the period is $\frac{2\pi}n=\frac{2\pi}3$ s.

In $30\pi$ s the number of full oscillations is $\frac{30\pi}{2\pi/3}=45$. Each oscillation covers $4A=8$ m, so the distance is $45\times8=360$ m.

questions.question:
An object of mass $5$ kg moves in simple harmonic motion with $v^2=27-18x-9x^2$ (centre $x=-1$, $n=3$, amplitude $2$ m).

Find the maximum force that acts on the object throughout its motion.
questions.answer:
$\ddot x=-n^2(x-c)=-9(x+1)$. The force is greatest at the extreme positions, where $|x+1|=2$: $|\ddot x|=9\times2=18$ m s$^{-2}$.

Maximum force $=5\times18=90$ N.

questions.question:
The equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+3b=0$, where $b$ and $c$ are real, has a complex root $b+ic$ (with $c\neq0$).

Using the relationship between the roots and the coefficients, show that the equation has a real root of $-3b$.
questions.answer:
The coefficients are real, so $b-ic$ is also a root. Let the third root be $\alpha$.

Sum of roots $=-b$: $(b-ic)+(b+ic)+\alpha=-b\Rightarrow\alpha=-3b$.

questions.question:
The equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+3b=0$, where $b$ and $c$ are real and $c\ne0$, has roots $b+ic$, $b-ic$ and $-3b$.

Using the relationship between the roots and the coefficients, find the possible values of $b$ and $c$.
questions.answer:
Sum of products of pairs $=c$:
$-3b(b-ic)-3b(b+ic)+(b-ic)(b+ic)=c\Rightarrow-6b^2+b^2+c^2=c\Rightarrow c^2-5b^2=c$ (1).

Product of roots $=-3b$: $-3b(b^2+c^2)=-3b\Rightarrow b(b^2+c^2-1)=0$.

Case $b=0$: (1) gives $c^2=c$, so $c=1$ (as $c\ne0$). 

Case $b\ne0$: $b^2+c^2=1$ (2). Substituting $b^2=1-c^2$ into (1): $c^2-5(1-c^2)=c\Rightarrow6c^2-c-5=0\Rightarrow(c-1)(6c+5)=0$, so $c=1$ (then $b=0$, contradicting $b\neq0$) or $c=-\frac56$, giving $b^2=1-\frac{25}{36}=\frac{11}{36}$, $b=\pm\frac{\sqrt{11}}6$.

Solutions: $(b,c)=(0,1)$ or $\left(\pm\frac{\sqrt{11}}6,-\frac56\right)$.

(The paper's solution divides by $b$ without treating $b=0$ separately; its final answers are the same.)

questions.question: Prove that the statement 'If $n$ is a multiple of $6$, then $\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^n$ is real' is true.
questions.answer:
$1-i\sqrt3=2\left(\cos\left(-\frac\pi3\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac\pi3\right)\right)$, so by de Moivre's theorem $\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^n=2^n\left(\cos\left(-\frac{n\pi}3\right)+i\sin\left(-\frac{n\pi}3\right)\right)$.

If $n=6m$ for an integer $m$, the argument is $-2m\pi$, so the result is $2^{6m}(\cos(-2m\pi)+i\sin(-2m\pi))=2^{6m}$, which is real.

questions.question: For the statement 'If $n$ is a multiple of $6$, then $\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^n$ is real', where $n$ is an integer, state the converse and determine if it is true, justifying your answer.
questions.answer:
Converse: 'If $\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^n$ is real, then $n$ is a multiple of $6$.'

$\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^n=2^n\left(\cos\frac{n\pi}3-i\sin\frac{n\pi}3\right)$ is real when $\sin\frac{n\pi}3=0$, i.e. whenever $n$ is a multiple of $3$. For example $n=3$: $\left(1-i\sqrt3\right)^3=-8$ is real but $3$ is not a multiple of $6$.

So the converse is false.

questions.question: Use integration by parts to find $\displaystyle\int e^x\cos2x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Let $I=\int e^x\cos2x\,dx$. With $u=\cos2x$, $v'=e^x$:

$I=e^x\cos2x+2\int e^x\sin2x\,dx$.

Again by parts with $u=\sin2x$, $v'=e^x$: $\int e^x\sin2x\,dx=e^x\sin2x-2\int e^x\cos2x\,dx=e^x\sin2x-2I$.

So $I=e^x\cos2x+2e^x\sin2x-4I$, giving $5I=e^x\cos2x+2e^x\sin2x+c$ and

$I=\frac15e^x\left(\cos2x+2\sin2x\right)+C$.

questions.question:
The quadrilateral $OABC$ has $OA=BA$ and $OC=BC$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$.

Use the fact that $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b-\mathbf a|$ to show that $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$.
questions.answer:
$|\mathbf a|^2=|\mathbf b-\mathbf a|^2\Rightarrow\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a=(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b-2\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a$.

Hence $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$.

questions.question:
The quadrilateral $OABC$ has $OA=BA$ and $OC=BC$. Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$. It is known that $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=2\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$.

Use vector methods to show that $OB\perp AC$.
questions.answer:
Similarly, from $OC=BC$, i.e. $|\mathbf c|=|\mathbf b-\mathbf c|$: $\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=2\,\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c$.

$\overrightarrow{OB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf c-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\frac12\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b-\frac12\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=0.$

Hence $OB\perp AC$.

questions.question:
By considering the expansion of $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^4$, show that
$$\tan4\theta=\frac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}.$$
questions.answer:
By the binomial theorem,
$(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^4=\cos^4\theta+4i\cos^3\theta\sin\theta-6\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta-4i\cos\theta\sin^3\theta+\sin^4\theta$.

By de Moivre's theorem this equals $\cos4\theta+i\sin4\theta$. Equating real and imaginary parts:

$\cos4\theta=\cos^4\theta-6\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta+\sin^4\theta$, $\sin4\theta=4\cos^3\theta\sin\theta-4\cos\theta\sin^3\theta$.

$\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\cos^3\theta\sin\theta-4\cos\theta\sin^3\theta}{\cos^4\theta-6\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta+\sin^4\theta}$. Dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos^4\theta$ gives
$\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}$.

questions.question: Given that $\tan4\theta=\dfrac{4\tan\theta-4\tan^3\theta}{1-6\tan^2\theta+\tan^4\theta}$, find the roots of the polynomial $x^4-4x^3-6x^2+4x+1=0$.
questions.answer:
Put $\tan4\theta=-1$: $-1=\dfrac{4t-4t^3}{1-6t^2+t^4}$ where $t=\tan\theta$. Then $-1+6t^2-t^4=4t-4t^3$, so $t^4-4t^3-6t^2+4t+1=0$.

So the roots of the polynomial are $x=\tan\theta$ where $\tan4\theta=-1$.

$4\theta=\frac{3\pi}4,\frac{7\pi}4,\frac{11\pi}4,\frac{15\pi}4$, so $\theta=\frac{3\pi}{16},\frac{7\pi}{16},\frac{11\pi}{16},\frac{15\pi}{16}$ (four distinct tangent values).

The roots are $\tan\frac{3\pi}{16},\ \tan\frac{7\pi}{16},\ \tan\frac{11\pi}{16},\ \tan\frac{15\pi}{16}$.

questions.question:
On a distant planet, an object of mass $m$ kg experiences a resistive force of $mkv^2$ when it moves through the atmosphere, where $v$ is its velocity and $k$ is a positive constant. The magnitude of acceleration due to gravity is $G$ m s$^{-2}$.

When falling, the equation of motion is $\ddot x=-G+kv^2$, and the object has a terminal velocity of $40$ m s$^{-1}$ in the negative direction.

Show that $\sqrt{\dfrac Gk}=40$.
questions.answer: At terminal velocity $\ddot x=0$ with $v=-40$: $0=-G+k(-40)^2$, so $\dfrac Gk=40^2$ and $\sqrt{\dfrac Gk}=40$.

questions.question:
On a distant planet, an object of mass $m$ kg experiences a resistive force of $mkv^2$ (with $k>0$) and gravity has magnitude $G$ m s$^{-2}$, where $\sqrt{G/k}=40$.

The object is projected upwards with a velocity of $40$ m s$^{-1}$. When it is moving upwards its equation of motion is $\ddot x=-G-kv^2$.

Show that $v=40\tan\left(\dfrac\pi4-40kt\right)$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-(G+kv^2)=-k(40^2+v^2)$ (using $G=1600k$).

$\int\frac{dv}{40^2+v^2}=-k\int dt\Rightarrow\frac1{40}\tan^{-1}\frac v{40}=-kt+c$.

At $t=0$, $v=40$: $c=\frac1{40}\tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{160}$.

$\tan^{-1}\frac v{40}=\frac\pi4-40kt\Rightarrow v=40\tan\left(\frac\pi4-40kt\right)$.

questions.question:
An object is projected upwards with velocity $40$ m s$^{-1}$ on a planet where $G/k=40^2$, and its velocity while moving upwards is $v=40\tan\left(\dfrac\pi4-40kt\right)$.

The object takes $4$ seconds to reach its maximum height. Calculate the exact value of $G$.
questions.answer:
At maximum height $v=0$ when $t=4$: $\tan\left(\frac\pi4-160k\right)=0$, so $\frac\pi4-160k=0$ and $k=\frac\pi{640}$.

$G=40^2k=1600\times\frac\pi{640}=\frac{5\pi}2$ m s$^{-2}$.

questions.question:
Write $\text{cis}\,\theta=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$. Show that $\text{cis}\,\theta+\text{cis}(-\theta)=2\cos\theta$.

(The original paper wrote this as $e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}=2\cos\theta$.)
questions.answer: $\text{cis}\,\theta+\text{cis}(-\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta+\cos(-\theta)+i\sin(-\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta+\cos\theta-i\sin\theta=2\cos\theta$, since cosine is even and sine is odd.

questions.question:
Two complex numbers lie on the unit circle: $z_1=\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha$ and $z_2=\cos\beta+i\sin\beta$, where $0\le\alpha\le\pi$ and $0\le\beta\le\pi$. (Write $\text{cis}\,\theta=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.) Given that $\text{cis}\,\theta+\text{cis}(-\theta)=2\cos\theta$.

The complex number $z_3$ is defined by $z_3=\dfrac1{z_1+z_2}$. For certain values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, $z_3$ has modulus $\dfrac1{\sqrt3}$.

Using the fact that $\text{cis}\,\alpha+\text{cis}\,\beta=\text{cis}\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\left(\text{cis}\frac{\alpha-\beta}2+\text{cis}\left(-\frac{\alpha-\beta}2\right)\right)$, or otherwise, find the possible values of $\alpha-\beta$.
questions.answer:
$|z_3|=\frac1{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow|z_1+z_2|=\sqrt3$.

$|z_1+z_2|=\left|\text{cis}\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\right|\left|\text{cis}\frac{\alpha-\beta}2+\text{cis}\left(-\frac{\alpha-\beta}2\right)\right|=1\times\left|2\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}2\right|$.

So $\left|\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}2\right|=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Since $0\le\alpha,\beta\le\pi$, $-\frac\pi2\le\frac{\alpha-\beta}2\le\frac\pi2$, so $\frac{\alpha-\beta}2=\pm\frac\pi6$.

Hence $\alpha-\beta=\pm\frac\pi3$.

questions.question: Use mathematical induction to show that $x+1$ is a factor of $x^n+1$ for all odd positive integers $n$.
questions.answer:
Let $P(n)$: $x^n+1$ is divisible by $x+1$, for odd $n$.

Base case $n=1$: $x+1=1\cdot(x+1)$, true.

Assume $P(k)$ for some odd $k$: $x^k+1=M(x+1)$ for some polynomial $M$, so $x^k=M(x+1)-1$.

Then $x^{k+2}+1=x^2x^k+1=x^2\left(M(x+1)-1\right)+1=Mx^2(x+1)-(x^2-1)=Mx^2(x+1)-(x+1)(x-1)=(x+1)\left(Mx^2-x+1\right)$, so $P(k+2)$ is true.

Since $k+2$ is the next odd integer, by induction $x+1$ is a factor of $x^n+1$ for all odd positive integers $n$.

questions.question:
It is known that for some $n,k,m\in\mathbb Z^+$, $n=m\times2^k$.

Use proof by contraposition to show that if $n$ is not a power of $2$, then $m$ has an odd factor larger than $1$.
questions.answer:
The contrapositive is: 'If $m$ does not have an odd factor larger than $1$, then $n$ is a power of $2$.'

Suppose $m$ has no odd factor larger than $1$. Then the only prime factor of $m$ is $2$, so $m=2^j$ for some integer $j\ge0$. Then $n=2^j\times2^k=2^{j+k}$, which is a power of $2$.

The contrapositive is proved, so the original statement is true.

questions.question:
Given (i) that $x+1$ is a factor of $x^n+1$ for all odd positive integers $n$, and (ii) that if $n$ is not a power of $2$ then $n=m\times2^k$ where $m$ has an odd factor larger than $1$:

Deduce that if $2^n+1$ is prime, then $n$ is a power of $2$.
questions.answer:
Contrapositive: if $n$ is not a power of $2$, then $2^n+1$ is not prime.

Suppose $n$ is not a power of $2$. By (ii), $n$ has an odd factor $a>1$, so $n=ab$ with $a$ odd, $a>1$ and $b\ge1$.

Then $2^n+1=(2^b)^a+1$. Putting $x=2^b$ in (i) (as $a$ is odd), $2^b+1$ divides $(2^b)^a+1=2^n+1$.

Also $2^b+1>1$ and, since $a>1$, $2^b+1<2^{ab}+1=2^n+1$. So $2^n+1$ has a factor strictly between $1$ and itself and is not prime.

By contraposition, if $2^n+1$ is prime then $n$ is a power of $2$.

questions.question:
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^n dx$ for integers $n\ge0$.

Use integration by parts to show that $I_n=\dfrac n{n+2}I_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$.
questions.answer:
Take $u=\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^n$, $v'=1$, so $u'=n\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^{n-1}\cdot\left(-\frac1{2\sqrt x}\right)$ and $v=x$:

$I_n=\Big[x\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^n\Big]_0^1+\frac n2\int_0^1\sqrt x\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^{n-1}dx$.

The bracket is $0$ (at $x=1$ the factor is $0$; at $x=0$ the factor $x$ is $0$). Write $\sqrt x=1-\left(1-\sqrt x\right)$:

$I_n=\frac n2\int_0^1\left(1-\left(1-\sqrt x\right)\right)\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^{n-1}dx=\frac n2\left(I_{n-1}-I_n\right)$.

So $I_n\left(1+\frac n2\right)=\frac n2I_{n-1}$, i.e. $I_n=\dfrac n{n+2}I_{n-1}$.

questions.question:
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(1-\sqrt x\right)^n dx$, with $I_n=\dfrac n{n+2}I_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$.

Hence show that $I_n=\dfrac2{(n+1)(n+2)}$.
questions.answer:
$I_0=\int_0^11\,dx=1$. Applying the recurrence repeatedly:

$I_n=\frac n{n+2}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n+1}\cdot\frac{n-2}{n}\cdot\frac{n-3}{n-1}\cdots\frac24\cdot\frac13\cdot I_0$.

Almost everything cancels, leaving $\dfrac{2\times1}{(n+2)(n+1)}$, so $I_n=\dfrac2{(n+1)(n+2)}$.

questions.question: Given that $I_n=\dfrac2{(n+1)(n+2)}$, by considering the partial fractions decomposition of $I_n$, or otherwise, deduce that $I_0+I_1+I_2+\cdots+I_n<2$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac2{(n+1)(n+2)}=\dfrac2{n+1}-\dfrac2{n+2}$.

So $I_0+I_1+\cdots+I_n=\left(\frac21-\frac22\right)+\left(\frac22-\frac23\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac2{n+1}-\frac2{n+2}\right)=2-\frac2{n+2}<2$.

questions.question:
Given that $p$ and $q$ are constants, use integration by substitution to show that
$$\int\frac{p-x}{\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}}\,dx=-\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}+c,$$
where $c$ is a constant.
questions.answer:
Let $u=(p-x)^2$, so $du=-2(p-x)\,dx$.

$\int\frac{p-x}{\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}}dx=-\frac12\int\left(q^2+u\right)^{-1/2}du=-\frac12\cdot2\left(q^2+u\right)^{1/2}+c=-\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}+c$.

questions.question:
An object of mass $1$ kg is suspended from the ceiling by two cables of equal length, attached to motors at points $A$ and $B$. The motors pull on their cables, creating a tension of $T$ newtons in each cable (constant at all times). The distance between $A$ and $B$ is $2k$ metres and the ceiling is $2k$ metres above the ground.

Let the height of the object above the ground be $x$ metres, the angle between each cable and the ceiling be $\theta$, and the magnitude of acceleration due to gravity be $10$ m s$^{-2}$.

Show that $\ddot x=\dfrac{2T(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}-10$.
questions.answer:
The object is horizontally midway between $A$ and $B$, so the horizontal components of the tensions cancel. The vertical component of each tension is $T\sin\theta$ upwards, and weight is $1\times10=10$ N downwards.

Each cable has horizontal run $k$ and vertical drop $2k-x$, so length $\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}$ and $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2k-x}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}$.

Newton's second law with $m=1$: $\ddot x=2T\sin\theta-10=\dfrac{2T(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}-10$.

questions.question:
An object of mass $1$ kg is suspended by two cables from points $A$ and $B$ on a ceiling $2k$ metres above the ground, with $AB=2k$ metres. Its height above the ground is $x$ metres and the tension in each cable is a constant $T$ newtons. Gravity is $10$ m s$^{-2}$. It is known that $\ddot x=\dfrac{2T(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}-10$.

The object is initially at rest on the ground. Using the result $\displaystyle\int\frac{p-x}{\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}}dx=-\sqrt{q^2+(p-x)^2}+c$, or otherwise, show that
$$(\dot x)^2=4T\left(k\sqrt5-\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}\right)-20x.$$
questions.answer:
$\frac d{dx}\left(\frac12v^2\right)=\ddot x=\frac{2T(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}-10$.

Integrating (using the given integral with $p=2k$, $q=k$): $\frac12v^2=-2T\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}-10x+c$, so $v^2=-4T\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}-20x+C$.

At $x=0$, $v=0$: $C=4T\sqrt{k^2+4k^2}=4Tk\sqrt5$.

Hence $(\dot x)^2=4T\left(k\sqrt5-\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}\right)-20x$.

questions.question:
An object of mass $1$ kg is suspended by two cables from a ceiling $2k$ metres above the ground, each with constant tension $T$ newtons. It starts at rest on the ground and its height $x$ satisfies $(\dot x)^2=4T\left(k\sqrt5-\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}\right)-20x$.

Show that if the object touches the ceiling, the minimum magnitude of the force produced by each motor is $T=5\varphi$ newtons, where $\varphi=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}2$.
questions.answer:
To reach the ceiling ($x=2k$) we need $(\dot x)^2\ge0$ there:

$4T\left(k\sqrt5-k\right)-40k\ge0\Rightarrow T\ge\frac{10}{\sqrt5-1}=\frac{10(\sqrt5+1)}{4}=5\cdot\frac{1+\sqrt5}2=5\varphi$.

So the minimum tension is $T=5\varphi$ N.

questions.question:
An object of mass $1$ kg is suspended by two cables from a ceiling $2k$ metres above the ground, each with constant tension $T$ newtons, where $\ddot x=\dfrac{2T(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}-10$ and $x$ is the height above the ground. When $T=5\varphi$ (with $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$) the object just touches the ceiling.

The maximum velocity of the object is reached when it has travelled a fraction $P$ of the distance between the floor and the ceiling. Given that $\varphi^2-1=\varphi$, show that $P=\dfrac{2\sqrt\varphi-1}{2\sqrt\varphi}$.
questions.answer:
Maximum velocity occurs when $\ddot x=0$. With $T=5\varphi$: $\dfrac{10\varphi(2k-x)}{\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}}=10$, so $\varphi(2k-x)=\sqrt{k^2+(2k-x)^2}$.

Square: $\varphi^2(2k-x)^2=k^2+(2k-x)^2\Rightarrow(2k-x)^2(\varphi^2-1)=k^2\Rightarrow(2k-x)^2=\dfrac{k^2}{\varphi}$ (using $\varphi^2-1=\varphi$).

Since $0\le x\le2k$: $2k-x=\dfrac k{\sqrt\varphi}$, so $x=2k-\dfrac k{\sqrt\varphi}=\dfrac{k(2\sqrt\varphi-1)}{\sqrt\varphi}$.

The fraction of the distance $2k$ travelled is $P=\dfrac xk\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{2\sqrt\varphi-1}{2\sqrt\varphi}$.

questions.question:
Let $f(x)$ be a function that is differentiable on the domain $x\in\left[\frac12,1\right]$.

Use integration by parts to show that
$$\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}f(\sin x)\,dx=\frac\pi6\left(3f(1)-f\left(\tfrac12\right)\right)-\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)\,dx.$$
questions.answer:
Take $u=f(\sin x)$, $v'=1$, so $u'=\cos x\,f'(\sin x)$, $v=x$:

$\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}f(\sin x)dx=\Big[xf(\sin x)\Big]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}-\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)dx$

$=\frac\pi2f(1)-\frac\pi6f\left(\frac12\right)-\int\cdots=\frac\pi6\left(3f(1)-f\left(\tfrac12\right)\right)-\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)dx$.

questions.question:
Given that, for $f$ differentiable on $\left[\frac12,1\right]$,
$$\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}f(\sin x)\,dx=\frac\pi6\left(3f(1)-f\left(\tfrac12\right)\right)-\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)\,dx,$$
hence find $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\frac{2\sin x+x\cos x}{\sqrt{\sin x}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Rearrange: $\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\left(f(\sin x)+x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)\right)dx=\frac\pi6\left(3f(1)-f\left(\frac12\right)\right)$.

Choose $f(x)=2\sqrt x$, so $f'(x)=\frac1{\sqrt x}$. Then $f(\sin x)+x\cos x\,f'(\sin x)=2\sqrt{\sin x}+\frac{x\cos x}{\sqrt{\sin x}}=\frac{2\sin x+x\cos x}{\sqrt{\sin x}}$.

So the integral is $\frac\pi6\left(3\cdot2-2\sqrt{\tfrac12}\right)=\frac\pi6\left(6-\sqrt2\right)$.

(The handwritten solution in the paper shows a minus sign in the integrand at one step; the integrand as printed in the question has a plus sign and the working above uses it. The final answer is the same.)

questions.question:
The AM–GM inequality states that for positive numbers $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$, $\dfrac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n}n\ge\sqrt[n]{x_1x_2\cdots x_n}$. (Do not prove this.)

Show that if $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ are positive numbers and $k_1,k_2,\dots,k_n$ are positive integers, then
$$\frac{a_1k_1+a_2k_2+\cdots+a_nk_n}{k_1+k_2+\cdots+k_n}\ge\left(a_1^{k_1}a_2^{k_2}\cdots a_n^{k_n}\right)^{\frac1{k_1+k_2+\cdots+k_n}}.$$
questions.answer:
Apply AM–GM to the $K=k_1+k_2+\cdots+k_n$ numbers consisting of $a_1$ repeated $k_1$ times, $a_2$ repeated $k_2$ times, …, $a_n$ repeated $k_n$ times:

$\dfrac{k_1a_1+k_2a_2+\cdots+k_na_n}{K}\ge\left(a_1^{k_1}a_2^{k_2}\cdots a_n^{k_n}\right)^{1/K}$.

questions.question:
For positive numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ and positive numbers $k_1,\dots,k_n$ (not necessarily integers) it is given that
$$\frac{a_1k_1+\cdots+a_nk_n}{k_1+\cdots+k_n}\ge\left(a_1^{k_1}\cdots a_n^{k_n}\right)^{\frac1{k_1+\cdots+k_n}}.$$
Show that if $a,b,c>0$ and $a+b+c=1$, then $a^ab^bc^c+a^bb^cc^a+a^cb^ac^b\le1$.
questions.answer:
Use the inequality with $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and weights $(k_1,k_2,k_3)$; here $k_1+k_2+k_3=a+b+c=1$.

1. $a_i=(a,b,c)$, $k_i=(a,b,c)$: $a^2+b^2+c^2\ge a^ab^bc^c$.
2. $a_i=(a,b,c)$, $k_i=(b,c,a)$: $ab+bc+ca\ge a^bb^cc^a$.
3. $a_i=(a,b,c)$, $k_i=(c,a,b)$: $ac+ba+cb\ge a^cb^ac^b$.

Adding: $a^ab^bc^c+a^bb^cc^a+a^cb^ac^b\le a^2+b^2+c^2+2(ab+bc+ca)=(a+b+c)^2=1$.

questions.question:
The paraboloid $x^2+y^2=kz$ ($k>0$) is shown. The curve $\mathbf r_1$ (dashed) spirals anticlockwise (viewed from above) and $\mathbf r_2$ (dotted) spirals clockwise. Point $P$ on $\mathbf r_1$ and point $Q$ on $\mathbf r_2$ are parametrised by $P\left(p\cos p,\ p\sin p,\ \tfrac1kp^2\right)$ and $Q\left(q\cos q,\ -q\sin q,\ \tfrac1kq^2\right)$, where $p,q\ge0$.

The point $R_n$ is the $n$th point of intersection of the curves $\mathbf r_1$ and $\mathbf r_2$ above the $xy$-plane.

Find, in terms of $n$, the value of the parameter $p$ that corresponds to the point $R_n$.
questions.answer:
At an intersection, $P=Q$. Equal $z$-coordinates give $p=q$ (both non-negative). The $x$-coordinates then agree automatically. The $y$-coordinates require $p\sin p=-p\sin p$, so $p\sin p=0$. Above the $xy$-plane, $p>0$, so $\sin p=0$ and $p=\pi,2\pi,3\pi,\dots$

Hence $R_n$ corresponds to $p=n\pi$.

questions.question:
The paraboloid $x^2+y^2=kz$ ($k>0$) contains the spiral curves $\mathbf r_1$: $\left(p\cos p,\ p\sin p,\ \tfrac1kp^2\right)$ and $\mathbf r_2$: $\left(q\cos q,\ -q\sin q,\ \tfrac1kq^2\right)$ with $p,q\ge0$. They intersect above the $xy$-plane at points $R_n$ ($n=1,2,3,\dots$) with parameter $p=q=n\pi$.

For all integers $n\ge1$, $\overrightarrow{R_nR_{n+1}}\perp\overrightarrow{R_{n+1}R_{n+2}}$. Find the exact value of $k$.
questions.answer:
$R_n=\left(n\pi\cos n\pi,\ 0,\ \frac{\pi^2n^2}k\right)$ and $R_{n+1}=\left(-(n+1)\pi\cos n\pi,\ 0,\ \frac{\pi^2(n+1)^2}k\right)$ (since $\cos(n+1)\pi=-\cos n\pi$).

$\overrightarrow{R_nR_{n+1}}=\begin{pmatrix}-(2n+1)\pi\cos n\pi\\0\\ \frac{\pi^2}k(2n+1)\end{pmatrix}$, and replacing $n$ by $n+1$:

$\overrightarrow{R_{n+1}R_{n+2}}=\begin{pmatrix}(2n+3)\pi\cos n\pi\\0\\ \frac{\pi^2}k(2n+3)\end{pmatrix}$.

Dot product $=0$: $-(2n+1)(2n+3)\pi^2\cos^2n\pi+\dfrac{\pi^4}{k^2}(2n+1)(2n+3)=0$.

With $\cos^2n\pi=1$ and dividing by $(2n+1)(2n+3)\pi^2$: $\dfrac{\pi^2}{k^2}=1$, so $k=\pi$ (as $k>0$).

questions.question:
The paraboloid $x^2+y^2=\pi z$ contains the spiral curves $\mathbf r_1$: $\left(p\cos p,\ p\sin p,\ \tfrac1\pi p^2\right)$ and $\mathbf r_2$: $\left(q\cos q,\ -q\sin q,\ \tfrac1\pi q^2\right)$, which intersect above the $xy$-plane at the points $R_n$ ($n\ge1$), with parameter $p=q=n\pi$. The tangent to $\mathbf r_1$ at $P$ has direction $\begin{pmatrix}-p\sin p+\cos p\\p\cos p+\sin p\\ \frac2\pi p\end{pmatrix}$ and the tangent to $\mathbf r_2$ at $Q$ has direction $\begin{pmatrix}-q\sin q+\cos q\\-q\cos q-\sin q\\ \frac2\pi q\end{pmatrix}$.

Let $\theta_n$ be the obtuse angle between the two tangents at $R_n$. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\tan\left(\frac{\theta_n}2\right)$.
questions.answer:
At $R_n$ ($p=q=n\pi$, $\sin n\pi=0$, $\cos n\pi=\pm1$):

$\mathbf d_1=\begin{pmatrix}\cos n\pi\\ n\pi\cos n\pi\\2n\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf d_2=\begin{pmatrix}\cos n\pi\\ -n\pi\cos n\pi\\2n\end{pmatrix}$.

$\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2=\cos^2n\pi-n^2\pi^2\cos^2n\pi+4n^2=1-n^2\pi^2+4n^2$, and $|\mathbf d_1|^2=|\mathbf d_2|^2=1+n^2\pi^2+4n^2$.

$\cos\theta_n=\dfrac{1+4n^2-n^2\pi^2}{1+4n^2+n^2\pi^2}$ (negative for large $n$ since $\pi^2>4$, so this is the obtuse angle).

$\tan^2\frac{\theta_n}2=\dfrac{1-\cos\theta_n}{1+\cos\theta_n}=\dfrac{2n^2\pi^2}{2(1+4n^2)}=\dfrac{n^2\pi^2}{1+4n^2}$.

As $\theta_n$ is obtuse, $\frac{\theta_n}2$ is acute, so $\tan\frac{\theta_n}2=\dfrac{n\pi}{\sqrt{1+4n^2}}=\dfrac\pi{\sqrt{\frac1{n^2}+4}}\to\dfrac\pi{\sqrt4}=\dfrac\pi2$.

$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\tan\frac{\theta_n}2=\frac\pi2$.
